_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 1 What Is an Algorithm? Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (Robo needs steps; algorithms all around; following an algorithm; making an algorithm; computers follow algorithms; the same steps, every time), in the lesson's own words and with the lesson's own drawings: the toast demo's five steps, ART.scene dress and teeth for the everyday algorithms, ART.scene handwash built one step at a time, ART.scene tower and plant for the ordering steps (and each of them in the WRONG order, which the kit's own scene draws), and ART.figure laptop for the program.
title: What Is an Algorithm?
subtitle: Grade 1 Computing
objectives: Know that an algorithm is a set of instructions to complete a task or to solve a problem.
Follow the steps in algorithms for everyday tasks.
Suggest sets of ordered instructions to complete simple tasks, such as drawing a picture of a particular object or building a brick tower.
Know that the order of instructions is important when creating algorithms.
Know that algorithms can be recreated as code on computers.

beats.say: A job done in steps, one after another, is an algorithm.
You follow algorithms every day. So does a computer.
Robo wants toast. But Robo cannot guess.
Robo only does what it is told. You tell it every step.
Take the bread. Put it in the toaster. Push the lever down.
Wait for it to pop up. Then spread the butter.
Toast! Those five steps are an algorithm: a set of steps to do a job.
Algorithms are not only for robots. You follow them every day.
Getting dressed is one. Socks, then shoes, then your coat.
Brushing your teeth is one. Paste on the brush. Brush. Rinse.
A recipe is one. So is a dance: step, step, clap, turn.
An algorithm does not have to be hard. Three steps can be enough.
To follow an algorithm you do step one, then step two, then step three.
You never skip a step, and you never jump ahead.
Here are five steps for washing your hands. Turn the tap on.
Soap. Rub your hands together. Rinse the bubbles away.
Dry them. Five steps, in order, and your hands are clean.
You can write an algorithm too. Think what has to happen first.
Build a tower. The big brick goes at the bottom, or the tower falls.
Then the middle brick, then the small one. The flag goes on last.
Start with the flag, and it has nothing under it. It lands on the floor.
Now plant a seed. Get a pot, put soil in it, plant the seed, water it.
Water it first? Water what? There is no seed yet.
Lots of people follow algorithms at work. A cook follows a recipe.
A builder follows a plan. A nurse follows steps to check you are well.
A computer follows algorithms too. Somebody always writes the steps.
The steps are written in code, and then the algorithm is a program.
An algorithm gives the same answer every time.
Clean your teeth this way on Monday. Do it again on Friday.
Your teeth get clean both times. That is why we write algorithms down.
Anybody can pick it up, follow it, and get the same result.
An algorithm is a set of steps to do a job, or to solve a problem.
You follow one step at a time, and when you write one the order has to work.
Written in code, your algorithm is a program a computer can run.
